<reason>PRO (Side B) won by repeatedly turning CON's own material against it: the recent soft landing CON cited as "patience working" was, as PRO noted, rates rising ~5 points with unemployment barely moving—i.e., the motion's cost as written. PRO's pressure question exposed a real tension in CON's case (workers "could not force catch-up raises" vs. inflation "lets wages catch up later"), and CON's "both can be true" answer, while plausible, left PRO able to argue that either the "spread" burden is a permanent real wage cut on the weak or the catch-up is exactly the second-round drift PRO warns of. Most damaging, CON's A1 defined patience as "raise to restrain demand, then pause once real wages are falling," which PRO credibly framed as the motion itself, narrowing the dispute to "the last point" of inflation. CON's strongest line—the concentrated, scarring harm of job loss versus thin inflation harm—stayed live and was well-expressed, and CON did extract a binding one-point definition of "modest." But attacking a one-point rise as "not modest" fights the motion's premise rather than the comparison, and CON never fully answered why holding at 3–4% for three years under continued tariff/deficit pressure would not erode the anchor. PRO's closing was clipped, a small execution cost, but it still crystallized the decisive comparison more cleanly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 turn on CON's history ([B2.1]-[B2.3]): "CON is citing the price of my policy to argue against my policy," followed up in Rebuttal 2 and Closing when CON's own definition of patience ([A4.1]) was shown to be essentially the motion, leaving only "the last point" as the live disagreement.</best_rebuttal>
